# Rough Idle Only When in Drive with AC On

A rough idle that manifests exclusively when a vehicle is in Drive with the Air Conditioning engaged, yet remains perfectly smooth in Park or Neutral, points to a specific set of mechanical and electronic interactions. The fact that the engine RPMs appear steady despite the vibration suggests the issue lies in load management rather than a catastrophic failure of the combustion process. When the transmission is shifted into Drive, the torque converter begins to lock up or circulate fluid, creating a baseline load on the crankshaft. Simultaneously, engaging the AC compressor adds a sudden, significant mechanical drag. The engine control unit (ECU) must instantly compensate for this combined load to maintain idle speed. If the compensation is delayed or insufficient, the engine struggles, resulting in that shuddering sensation at a stoplight.

The most common culprit in vehicles of this era, such as the 2010 Ford Escape mentioned in your scenario, is the Idle Air Control (IAC) valve or the Electronic Throttle Body (ETB). These components manage airflow when the throttle plate is closed. Over time, carbon buildup can restrict the precise movement required to bypass the throttle plate and increase RPMs under load. While the AC runs fine and provides cold air, indicating the compressor clutch and refrigerant levels are likely adequate, the actuation of the clutch still imposes a physical torque spike. If the IAC valve is clogged or its stepper motor is failing to respond quickly enough to the ECU's command, the engine will dip in RPM before recovering, causing instability.

Another critical component to investigate is the Idle Control Motor (ICM) found on many Ford vehicles from this period. Unlike older mechanical IAC valves, the ICM is an electric motor integrated into the throttle body that adjusts airflow electronically. If the ICM is sluggish or its position sensor is drifting, the ECU may be unable to maintain the target idle speed when the AC engages. Technicians often find that cleaning the throttle body and replacing the ICM resolves these "drive-mode" specific issues without needing a full engine overhaul.

It is also worth considering the torque converter lockup solenoid. In some configurations, if the transmission fails to manage the fluid coupling correctly under heavy load (AC + Drive), it can cause excessive slip or drag that mimics an idle issue. However, since you noted the shaking occurs specifically while waiting at a light and not during acceleration, the engine's ability to handle load is the primary concern.

Dealership recommendations to consider this "normal" often stem from outdated service bulletins or a lack of specific diagnostic data for these symptoms. A rough idle that degrades drivability at a stoplight is not acceptable wear; it indicates a control loop error. The ECU expects the engine to be in Park when the AC engages to minimize load, or it expects the IAC to compensate instantly. When neither occurs, the vehicle feels unstable.

To address this effectively, request a scan for pending codes and freeze frame data. Even if no check engine light is illuminated, the ECU may have stored codes related to throttle actuator control or idle air control performance. Furthermore, ask for a live data stream review while the AC is turned on. You should see the IAC duty cycle or ICM position jumping significantly when the compressor clicks in. If the RPM target hits but the actual RPM lags, the hardware is likely worn. Cleaning the throttle body is a low-cost first step, but if the issue persists, replacing the Idle Control Motor is the standard repair procedure for this specific symptom cluster.
